Added in 4.10.0. `internal/notify` is the first increment of Phase 2 of the
plan of record, whose own acceptance bar for this phase is literally "a 03:00
alarm pages a phone." It registers with `alarm.Engine`'s existing
`OnTransition` hook and, when an alarm is **raised**, sends a notification
through every configured, enabled channel whose priority floor the alarm
meets. Off by default (`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_ENABLED`): a deployment with nobody to
page has nothing to configure this against.

## Why only "raised"

`alarm.Engine.OnTransition` fires on every ISA-18.2 transition, raised,
cleared, acked, shelved, unshelved. This package listens to all of them but
acts on exactly one. Paging on every transition would mean an operator's
phone buzzing when they acknowledge their own alarm, when it clears on its
own, when someone shelves it for a shift, training them to swipe pages away
unread the same way a chattering alarm trains them to ignore alarms. Raised
is the one event that means "something needs a human who might not already be
looking at a screen," which is the entire reason this package exists.

The one other page is an escalation: the alarm was raised, nobody has
acknowledged it, and the policy says to tell the next person. It's the same
alarm still needing somebody, said again to someone else, not a new event. See
"Escalation".

One case that looks like an unshelve is really a raise. If the condition comes
up while an alarm is shelved, nobody has been told, so when the shelve ends
(timed out or unshelved by hand) the engine records the unshelve and then a
raise, and the raise pages. An alarm that was already in alarm when it was
shelved and still is comes back unacknowledged but doesn't page again: it paged
the first time.

## The channels

Six, and that's the list (see "Notifications" in [ROADMAP.md](/roadmap/) for
what we're not doing and why). Every one needs no vendor SDK and no paid
account, matching this project's plan of record: cloud integrations are opt-in
outbound connections an operator configures, never something this app requires
to run.

- **ntfy**: a push to a phone, with an **Acknowledge** button that acks the
  alarm straight back into HotLoop. Free, and you can run the server on the
  plant network with no internet at all. See "Setting up ntfy".
- **Gotify**: a push to a phone. Free, self-hosted, works with no internet.
  No buttons and no iPhone app, so it's a pager, not a two-way. See "Setting
  up Gotify".
- **Discord webhook**: an embed in a Discord channel, colored by priority,
  with the tag, value, limit, area and line. Paste a URL and it works. Critical
  alarms can ping a role. No buttons. See "Discord".
- **Discord bot**: the same message, with **Acknowledge** and **Shelve**
  buttons that act on the alarm and record who pressed them. The presses come
  back over a connection HotLoop opens to Discord, so the plant needs no public
  address. See "Discord".

- **Webhook**: a POST of HotLoop's own JSON body (`alarmId`, `name`,
  `priority`, `priorityLabel`, `message`, `deviceId`, `tagName`, `raisedAt`,
  `event`, which is `raised`, or `escalated` for an escalation) to a configured URL. It works with anything that takes whatever
  JSON you send it: your own script behind a small HTTP listener, Node-RED, n8n,
  or a "catch any webhook" trigger in a workflow tool. (Pointed at an ntfy
  topic it pages, with the raw JSON as the text; use the ntfy channel above
  instead.) A summary (see "Rate limits and summaries") has `event`
  `summary` and an `alarms` list naming every alarm in it. It does not work with services that want the body in their own
  shape. Discord answers 400 because there's no `content` or `embeds`. Slack,
  Teams and Google Chat want their own text field. Pushover wants its `token`,
  `user` and `message` fields, and PagerDuty's Events API wants a
  `routing_key`, an `event_action` and a `payload`. Point the webhook at one of
  those and every page fails. Discord has channels of its own that build the
  body Discord expects; use those.
- **Email over SMTP**: sent through whatever relay an operator already has
  (a corporate mail server, a transactional-email provider's SMTP endpoint, a
  self-hosted relay). No API key, no vendor library: `net/smtp` and a
  hand-built plain-text message. Many phones already surface email as a push
  notification on their own, and many paging tools accept an email-to-SMS
  bridge address as a "contact method", so this one channel alone covers a
  meaningful slice of "pages a phone" with zero paid dependency.

## The webhook URL is never printed

For a lot of receivers the URL is the password. Discord puts the token in the
path (`/api/webhooks/{id}/{token}`), ntfy takes it as `?auth=`, Google Chat as
`?key=` and `?token=`. Anyone holding the URL can post to your channel. So when
a send fails, the error names the scheme and host and nothing else:

```
webhook request to https://discord.com failed: context deadline exceeded
webhook https://ntfy.example.com returned 401 Unauthorized
```

That's the same text in the log, in the audit event and in the
`POST /api/notify/test` response. The host is enough to tell which receiver
broke; the path and the query never leave the process. A URL that fails
validation at startup isn't repeated in that error either. If you need to see
the URL, look at `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_WEBHOOK_URL` where you set it.

## Setting up ntfy

[ntfy](https://ntfy.sh) is a publish/subscribe push server. HotLoop publishes
each alarm to a topic; the ntfy app on the phone subscribes to it.

1. Run a server, or use ntfy.sh. On a plant network, run your own
   (`binwiederhier/ntfy`, one container) and lock it down: set
   `auth-default-access: deny-all`, create a user for HotLoop that may write
   the topic, and one per person that may read it. On ntfy.sh, or any server
   anyone can reach, **the topic name is the password**: anybody who guesses it
   reads your alarms. Make it long and random.
2. Give HotLoop an access token (`ntfy token add hotloop`) or a username and
   password for that user.
3. Set `HOTLOOP_PUBLIC_URL` to the address a phone reaches HotLoop at, for
   example `https://hotloop.plant.example`. Without it the notification still
   arrives, but with no Acknowledge button and no tap-to-open, because the phone
   would have nowhere to send either.
4. Configure it and restart:

```
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_ENABLED=true
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_NTFY_ENABLED=true
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_NTFY_URL=https://ntfy.plant.example
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_NTFY_TOPIC=boiler-house-alarms
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_NTFY_TOKEN=tk_...
HOTLOOP_PUBLIC_URL=https://hotloop.plant.example
```

5. `POST /api/notify/test` sends a test notification. It has no Acknowledge
   button, because there's no alarm behind it to acknowledge.

The URL is the server alone. The topic goes in its own setting, never in the
URL: that way HotLoop knows which part is the secret and keeps it out of every
error, log line and audit event.

What arrives:

| <span class="sr-only">Details</span> | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|
| Title | The alarm's name |
| Body | The alarm's message, its priority, where it came from (`device/tag`) and when it was raised |
| Priority | Critical 5 (max: on Android it can break through do-not-disturb, if you let it), High 4, Medium 3, Low 2 |
| Tags | An emoji by severity and the priority as a word, so the list on the phone can be scanned |
| Tap | Opens HotLoop's alarm list, when `HOTLOOP_PUBLIC_URL` is set |
| Button | **Acknowledge**, when `HOTLOOP_PUBLIC_URL` is set. See "Acknowledge links" |

### The iPhone caveat

Android works with no internet at all: the ntfy app keeps its own connection to
your server and gets every message instantly over the plant Wi-Fi.

iPhones don't. Apple only lets a push through its own servers (APNs), and only
ntfy.sh can talk to APNs. A self-hosted server has to be configured with
`upstream-base-url: https://ntfy.sh`, and then it forwards a poll request (no
message content, just "something arrived on this topic") to ntfy.sh, which
wakes the phone, which then fetches the message from your server. So on a plant
with no internet, iPhones do not get instant notifications from a self-hosted
ntfy. They see them when the app is opened. If your people carry iPhones and
the plant is air-gapped, ntfy is not your pager; email through a relay is, or
Discord if the plant can reach it. Gotify has no iPhone app at all.

The Acknowledge button is a request from the phone to `HOTLOOP_PUBLIC_URL`, so
the phone has to be able to reach that address: on the plant Wi-Fi, or through
whatever VPN you use. It works the same on either platform.

## Setting up Gotify

[Gotify](https://gotify.net) is a small self-hosted push server with an Android
app. No internet needed, no account anywhere.

1. Run `gotify/server` and log in to its web UI.
2. Under **Apps**, create an application called HotLoop. Copy its token.
3. Configure it and restart:

```
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_ENABLED=true
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_GOTIFY_ENABLED=true
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_GOTIFY_URL=https://gotify.plant.example
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_GOTIFY_TOKEN=A...
HOTLOOP_PUBLIC_URL=https://hotloop.plant.example
```

The token goes in the `X-Gotify-Key` header, never as `?token=` in the URL,
where it would end up in every proxy's access log.

Priorities map onto what the Android app does with them: Critical 10 and High 8
are high importance (sound and a heads-up pop-up), Medium 5 is a normal
notification with sound, Low 2 is silent. The message is Markdown (the alarm's
name bold, the details as a list, the alarm's own text escaped so a name with an
asterisk in it reads as that name), and tapping it opens HotLoop's alarm list
when `HOTLOOP_PUBLIC_URL` is set.

**No acknowledge.** Gotify notifications have no action buttons, so there's no
way to put an Acknowledge button on one, and we won't fake it with a link that
acknowledges on a plain GET: link previewers and security scanners open links
on their own, and an alarm must never be acknowledged by a robot. Acknowledge
in HotLoop. **No iPhone app** either.

## Discord

Two ways in. The webhook is a pager: paste a URL, get alarms in a channel. The
bot is a two-way: the same messages with **Acknowledge** and **Shelve**
buttons, and the audit trail says which person pressed them. Both need the
plant to reach Discord over the internet (outbound HTTPS to `discord.com`, and
for the bot a WebSocket to `*.discord.gg`). Neither needs Discord to reach the
plant.

### What arrives

| <span class="sr-only">Details</span> | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|
| Text | `[Critical] Boiler Trip`, which is what a phone's push notification shows. On a Critical alarm, a ping of the configured role in front of it |
| Embed title | The same, linking to HotLoop's alarm list when `HOTLOOP_PUBLIC_URL` is set |
| Color | Critical red, High orange, Medium yellow, Low blue |
| Description | The alarm's message |
| Fields | Tag (`device/tag`), Value (the reading that raised it), Limit (`hi 90`, from the definition), Area / Line (from the device), Raised (in each reader's own time zone) |
| Footer | `HotLoop | <HOTLOOP_PLANT_NAME>`, so a server with several plants in it can tell them apart (just `HotLoop` when the plant name isn't set) |
| Buttons (bot only) | Acknowledge, Shelve 1h, Open in HotLoop |

A flood becomes a summary, the same as every other channel: the first five go
out, then one message listing the rest, as many names as fit and a count of
the others, so the count is never cut off.

Discord refuses a message that's too long (2000 characters of text, 256 of
title, 4096 of description, 25 fields, 6000 in all), and a refused message is a
page that didn't go out. So HotLoop cuts to fit, on a character boundary, with
`...` where it cut.

### Nobody gets pinged by accident

Every message goes out with `allowed_mentions: {"parse": []}`. Without it
Discord pings whatever the text mentions, so an alarm somebody named
"@everyone tank overflow" would wake the whole server. With it, nothing in the
text pings anyone. The one exception is the role you configure for Critical
(`..._CRITICAL_ROLE`), which is named explicitly as the only mention allowed, and
only on a Critical alarm or a summary with a Critical alarm in it. A test
notification never pings. The alarm's own text is Markdown-escaped too, so a
name with `*` in it reads as that name and a `<@&role>` in a name is shown, not
used.

For the ping to work the role has to be mentionable: in the server's role
settings turn on **Allow anyone to @mention this role**, or give the bot the
**Mention @everyone, @here, and All Roles** permission.

### Discord's rate limits and bans

Discord answers "too fast" with a 429 and says how long to wait, in the body
(`retry_after`, to the millisecond) and in `X-RateLimit-Reset-After`. That's
how long HotLoop waits before the retry, inside the usual three attempts and
30 seconds (see "Retries"). When Discord says the budget is spent before it
refuses (`X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0`), the next send waits for the reset
instead of drawing a 429.

Discord bans the address of anything that racks up 10,000 refused requests
(401, 403, 429) in ten minutes, and the ban takes every Discord integration on
that address with it. So when Discord answers **401, 403 or 404** (a wrong or
deleted webhook, a bad bot token, a channel the bot can't see), HotLoop
**switches that channel off** after that one request. It logs it once, every
alarm after that is refused without a request (and audited as not sent, so
"was anybody told" still has an answer), and it shows in `GET /api/diagnostics`
under `notify.channels`, with the reason and when:

```json
{"channel": "discord-webhook", "broken": true,
 "reason": "discord webhook https://discord.com returned 404 Not Found: Unknown Webhook (Discord error 10015)",
 "since": "2026-09-27T03:00:01Z"}
```

Fix the setting and restart HotLoop. A 500 or no answer at all doesn't switch
anything off; those are retried like any other channel's.

### Setting up the webhook

1. In Discord, open the channel's settings (the gear), **Integrations**,
   **Webhooks**, **New Webhook**. Name it HotLoop. **Copy Webhook URL**.
2. Optional: a role to ping on Critical. Turn on **Developer Mode** (User
   Settings, Advanced), then right-click the role in Server Settings, Roles,
   and **Copy Role ID**. It's a number, not a name.
3. Configure it and restart:

```
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_ENABLED=true
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_WEBHOOK_ENABLED=true
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL=https://discord.com/api/webhooks/1234.../AbCd...
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_WEBHOOK_CRITICAL_ROLE=123456789012345678
HOTLOOP_PUBLIC_URL=https://hotloop.plant.example
```

4. `POST /api/notify/test` sends a test message.

**The whole URL is the password.** Anyone holding it can post to your channel
as the webhook. HotLoop never prints it: not in the log, not in an error, not
in an audit event, not in an API response, and a URL that fails validation at
startup isn't repeated in that error either. In the Helm chart it goes into a
Secret. If it leaks, delete the webhook in Discord and make a new one.

A webhook can't carry a button that does anything, so there's no Acknowledge
here. The title links to the alarm list in HotLoop. For buttons, use the bot.

### Setting up the bot

1. Go to the [Discord developer portal](https://discord.com/developers/applications),
   **New Application**, call it HotLoop. The **Application ID** on the General
   Information page is what the invite link needs.
2. **Bot** tab: **Reset Token** and copy it. Discord shows it once. That's
   `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN`. On the same page turn **Public Bot**
   off, so nobody but you can add it to a server, and leave all three
   **Privileged Gateway Intents** off. HotLoop asks Discord for no events at
   all (intents 0); button presses arrive regardless.
3. Invite it to your server with the least it needs, View Channels, Send
   Messages and Embed Links (permissions `19456`), and no other scope than
   `bot`:

```
https://discord.com/oauth2/authorize?client_id=<APPLICATION ID>&scope=bot&permissions=19456
```

   Add **Mention @everyone, @here, and All Roles** (`permissions=150528`) only
   if the Critical role isn't mentionable and you'd rather not make it so.
   Editing its own message after a press needs no permission; that goes
   through the press itself.
4. The channel: with Developer Mode on, right-click it, **Copy Channel ID**. If
   the channel is private, add the bot's role to it.
5. The roles that may press the buttons. Make a role (say, "Alarm ack"), give
   it to the people who may acknowledge from Discord, and copy its id. Shelving
   takes an alarm off the list for an hour, so it has its own setting; it can
   be the same role or a narrower one.
6. Configure it and restart:

```
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_ENABLED=true
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_ENABLED=true
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN=MTIz...
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_CHANNEL=223456789012345678
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_ACK_ROLES=323456789012345678
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_SHELVE_ROLES=423456789012345678
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_CRITICAL_ROLE=323456789012345678
HOTLOOP_PUBLIC_URL=https://hotloop.plant.example
```

7. The log says `connected to the Discord Gateway; Discord buttons work`, and
   `GET /api/diagnostics` shows `"gateway": {"connected": true}` under the
   `discord` channel. `POST /api/notify/test` posts a test message (no
   buttons, there's no alarm behind it).

**Until you set the roles, nobody can press anything.** With
`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_ACK_ROLES` or `_SHELVE_ROLES` empty, every press of
that button is refused, the person pressing it is told which setting is empty,
and HotLoop says so at startup:

```
WARN NOBODY can acknowledge alarms from Discord, because HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_ACK_ROLES is empty...
```

That's on purpose. A button anyone in the server can press is not a default to
ship: servers collect people.

**Who pressed it.** An acknowledgement from Discord is recorded under
`discord:<username>#<user id>` (the id, because a Discord username can be
changed and the id can't), with the note "acknowledged from Discord by alice
(1010...)". To record it under the HotLoop user instead, map them:
`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_USERS=101010101010101010=alice,202020202020202020=bob`.
The mapping only names the actor. It doesn't check the HotLoop user's
permissions: the Discord role is what decides who may press.

**Shelve** shelves for `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_SHELVE`, one hour by
default, at most 24 hours like any shelve. It's a fixed time, not a menu:
at 03:00 one button that does one known thing beats a dropdown. It refuses an
alarm that's back to normal (shelving it would hide whatever trips it next)
and one that's already shelved.

After a press, the message says who did what and when, and both buttons go
gray, so the next person to look at the channel sees it's handled. A refused
press is answered only to the person who pressed it, with the reason, and
recorded in the system log.

### How a press is authorized

The same machinery as ntfy's Acknowledge link (see "Acknowledge links"), plus
Discord's own word on who pressed:

- **The button is signed.** Each button carries a token signed with the same
  secret as the ack links, for that action (acknowledge or shelve, signed in,
  so one can't be replayed as the other), on that alarm, raised at that
  moment. Discord allows a button 100 characters of data and an alarm id can
  be 64, so this is a compact form of the same claim: 8 bytes of raise time, 4
  of expiry and a 96-bit HMAC. Forging one means guessing 96 bits, one Discord
  press per guess, from inside the server with the right role.
- **The person holds a role you named.** Discord tells the bot the presser's
  roles with the press, over the bot's own authenticated connection. Anyone
  who can hand out roles in your server can hand out this one, so treat those
  roles like the permission they are.
- **The occurrence is still current.** The engine checks, under its own lock,
  that the alarm's current raise is the one on the button. Yesterday's message
  can't acknowledge today's trip.
- **Once.** The first action on an occurrence from any notification (ntfy or
  Discord) is recorded and every later one refused. Two people pressing at
  once: one wins, the other is told.
- **Expiring.** After `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_ACK_TTL` (12 hours) the buttons stop
  working; act in HotLoop instead.

The bot token is a credential for the whole bot. It is never logged, never in
an error, never in an API response; in the Helm chart it goes in a Secret. So
is each press's own interaction token, which Discord gives the bot for fifteen
minutes to answer it. If the bot token leaks, reset it in the developer
portal.

### The Gateway connection

Presses arrive over the Discord Gateway, a WebSocket HotLoop opens to Discord
and keeps open. The client is HotLoop's own, on
[gorilla/websocket](https://github.com/gorilla/websocket) (v1.5.3, pinned; it
was already in this module's dependency graph, it's small and it's the most
used WebSocket library in Go). We didn't take a Discord library such as
discordgo: it's a whole Discord SDK (REST, voice, a state cache) for the one
event we need, and this project doesn't carry vendor SDKs. The client:

- identifies with intents 0, so Discord sends it nothing but presses;
- heartbeats at the interval Discord gives, answers a heartbeat request at
  once, and treats a heartbeat that isn't acknowledged as a dead connection;
- resumes the session after a drop, a Reconnect (op 7) or a resumable Invalid
  Session (op 9), so a press made while it was reconnecting is replayed, not
  lost; a session that can't be resumed waits one to five seconds and starts
  a new one;
- identifies no more than once every five seconds, and not at all when
  Discord says the day's session starts are used up, until they reset;
- reconnects with a backoff that doubles from one second to a minute;
- stops for good on a refused token or refused intents, switches the channel
  off and shows it in `/api/diagnostics`, rather than reconnecting forever.

Discord gives the bot three seconds to answer a press, so the first thing
HotLoop does is answer "got it" (a deferred update), then does the work. That
answer is also what keeps two HotLoop replicas from both acting on one press:
both receive it, Discord takes the first answer and refuses the second, and
the replica that was refused stops. Run as an MCP helper (`--mcp-stdio`),
HotLoop doesn't open a Gateway connection at all; the real one handles the
presses.

### What's verified, and what needs a live run

Discord can't run in our lab, so the channels are tested against
`internal/notify/discordtest`: a real HTTP server standing in for Discord's REST
API, and a real WebSocket server speaking the Gateway frames the client uses,
both in the test process. It enforces Discord's documented limits and answers
the way Discord's documentation says Discord answers. **Tested** that way, in
CI:

- the exact JSON of a message, byte for byte; `allowed_mentions` locked to
  nothing, the role pinged only on Critical and never on a test, a mention in
  an alarm name escaped;
- every length limit kept, cut on a character boundary, with emoji; a summary
  of forty long-named alarms keeping its count;
- a 429 retried after the body's `retry_after` (not the whole-second
  `Retry-After` beside it) and after `X-RateLimit-Reset-After`; an empty bucket
  waited out before sending;
- 401, 403 and 404 each switching the channel off after exactly one request,
  logged once, shown in `/api/diagnostics`; a 500 and a refused connection not
  switching it off;
- a flood of twelve through the default budget: five messages, then one
  summary naming the other seven;
- no webhook URL, token, bot token, interaction token or button token in any
  error, log line, audit event or API response;
- the Gateway client, as protocol conformance: Identify with intents 0, the
  heartbeat interval, an immediate heartbeat on request, a clean 1000 close on
  shutdown; Reconnect resuming with the right session and sequence and getting
  the missed press replayed, closing with a code that keeps the session;
  Invalid Session both ways, with the wait and the identify gap; a zombie
  connection resumed; a dropped one resumed; 4009 starting a new session; 4014
  and a refused token stopping for good; the day's session starts waited out;
- end to end against the real alarm engine on a real Modbus register: the
  alarm raised, posted with its buttons, Acknowledge pressed as Discord sends
  it, and the real alarm acknowledged as `discord:alice#<id>`, the message
  edited to say so with its buttons off; Shelve pressed by a mapped user and
  the alarm shelved for the configured time under the HotLoop name; a forged
  button, a person without the role, a second press and a stale button from an
  earlier raise each refused, only to the presser, and in the system log; a
  bot with no roles set refusing everyone and saying so at startup.

What that proves: HotLoop sends what Discord documents and copes with every
answer Discord documents. What it can't: that Discord behaves as documented,
how the message looks in the Discord app, whether a push reaches a phone, and
the Gateway features this client never asks for (compression, sharding). Those
need a live run, and there are two, skipped unless you give them credentials:

```
# the webhook: sends a Critical, a High and a test message
HOTLOOP_TEST_DISCORD_WEBHOOK=https://discord.com/api/webhooks/...
HOTLOOP_TEST_DISCORD_ROLE=<role id to ping on the Critical one>   # optional
go test ./internal/notify/ -run TestDiscordWebhookLive -v

# the bot: connects to the real Gateway, raises a real alarm, posts it with
# buttons, and with PRESS_WAIT set waits for you to press Acknowledge
HOTLOOP_TEST_DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN=...
HOTLOOP_TEST_DISCORD_CHANNEL=<channel id>
HOTLOOP_TEST_DISCORD_ROLE=<role id you hold>
HOTLOOP_TEST_DISCORD_PRESS_WAIT=5m
go test ./internal/api/ -run TestDiscordBotLive -v
```

The bot test needs the database and the rest of the integration services like
every test in `internal/api`. **Not yet run live**: neither test has been run
against the real Discord as of this writing. Until it has, the Discord
channels are tested, not verified.

## Rate limits and summaries

A power dip or a PLC reboot trips forty alarms in a second. One send per alarm
gets a Discord webhook's IP banned, trips ntfy's per-IP limit, and buries the
one alarm that matters under thirty-nine that don't on the phone that gets them.
So every channel has a budget, a token bucket: a burst that may go out at once,
then one more every refill.

| Channel | Default burst | Then one every |
|---|---|---|
| ntfy | 10 | 5 s (under ntfy.sh's own limit of 60, then one per 5 s, per IP) |
| Gotify | 10 | 5 s |
| Webhook | 10 | 5 s |
| SMTP | 5 | 12 s |
| Discord webhook | 5 | 2 s (Discord allows a webhook about 5 requests every 2 s, and a channel 30 messages a minute) |
| Discord bot | 5 | 2 s |

Change them per channel with `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_<CHANNEL>_BURST` and
`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_<CHANNEL>_REFILL` (`WEBHOOK`, `SMTP`, `NTFY`, `GOTIFY`,
`DISCORD_WEBHOOK`, `DISCORD_BOT`).

What the budget allows goes out on its own, straight away. What it doesn't is
held, and when the next send is due everything held goes out as **one**
summary:

```
7 more alarms raised in the last 12 s:
- [High] Line 3 Stopped
- [Critical] Boiler Trip
...
```

No alarm is dropped: the summary names every one, up to 25, and counts the
rest ("...and 13 more"). It's as severe as the worst alarm in it, and the audit
event for it lists every alarm id it stood for. It has no Acknowledge button,
because there's no single alarm for it to acknowledge. If only one alarm was
held, it goes out as itself, button and all. Once alarms are being held, new
ones join the batch even if the budget has come back, so a summary never
arrives after an alarm raised later than everything in it. On shutdown, whatever
is still held goes out at once, over budget: the choice then is between one
send too many and alarms nobody is ever told about.

The budget is per channel, so a flood that has the SMTP relay queueing doesn't
hold up ntfy, and each channel's floor still applies: a Low alarm never ends up
in the summary of a channel set to High and above.

## Retries

A send that gets a 429, a 5xx, or no answer at all (refused, reset, timed out)
is tried again, up to three attempts in all, all inside 30 seconds of the first.
When the receiver says how long to wait (`Retry-After`, in seconds or as a
date), that's how long we wait; otherwise one second, then two. A receiver that
asks for longer than the 30 seconds has left is not waited on: the failure is
reported now, saying so. After 30 seconds a page that hasn't gone out is better
reported as failed, in the log and the audit trail, than retried quietly for
minutes while the alarm sits there.

Any other 4xx (a wrong token, a topic the user can't write, a malformed
request) is never retried. It'll be the same answer every time until somebody
fixes the configuration, and Discord bans an IP that keeps sending requests it
has already refused.

`POST /api/notify/test` makes exactly one attempt per channel. A test is asking
what the channel does right now, and a retry would make a flaky receiver look
fine.

## Acknowledge links

The Acknowledge button on an ntfy notification is a request to
`POST /api/notify/ack/{token}` on `HOTLOOP_PUBLIC_URL`. The person pressing it
at 03:00 isn't logged in to anything, so **the token is the whole
authorization**. That only works if the token is unforgeable, narrow, single use
and short-lived, and each of those is enforced:

- **Unforgeable.** The token is a claim (which alarm, when it was raised, which
  channel, when the link expires) plus an HMAC-SHA256 of it with a server
  secret. Change one byte, or sign with any other key, and it's refused. The
  secret is `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_ACK_SECRET` if you set it (32 characters at least;
  `openssl rand -hex 32`). If you don't, HotLoop generates 32 random bytes the
  first time it needs them and keeps them in its database (the `settings` table,
  key `notify.ackSecret`), so links keep working across a restart and every
  replica agrees. It's never shown on the settings screen or in any API
  response. It is in database backups, like everything else in the database; if
  that's a problem for you, set the variable from a Kubernetes Secret instead
  (`notify.ackSecret.existingSecret` in the chart), and it never touches the
  database. Changing the secret invalidates every link already sent, which is
  also how you revoke them all at once.
- **Narrow.** The claim names one alarm **and the moment it was raised**. A
  button from yesterday's trip of the same alarm can't acknowledge today's,
  which nobody has seen yet: the engine checks, under the same lock as the
  acknowledgement, that the alarm's current raise is the one in the claim
  (`alarm.Engine.AckOccurrence`). The link can acknowledge and nothing else. It
  can't shelve, clear, write a tag or read anything, so the worst a leaked link
  can do is exactly what pressing the button would have done.
- **Single use.** The first use of a link for an occurrence is recorded in the
  database (`notify_ack_links`), and every later use is refused, even when the
  alarm needs acknowledging again without a new raise (shelved while still in
  alarm and unshelved, it comes back unacknowledged). The alarm's own state
  isn't enough for this; the record is.
- **Short-lived.** It expires, 12 hours after it's sent by default
  (`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_ACK_TTL`, at most 168h). Long enough for "I'll look when I
  get in", short enough that a screenshot of a notification is not a standing
  credential.

A successful press is an ordinary ISA-18.2 acknowledgement through the alarm
engine, audited exactly like one from the alarm screen: an alarm event and a
system-log entry with the actor `notify:ntfy` and the note "acknowledged from
the ntfy notification". ntfy's HTTP actions don't say which phone pressed the
button, so there's no person's name to add. When several people share a topic,
the audit trail says the phone did it, not who. The Discord bot knows the user
and puts it there (see "Discord").

Every refusal is answered with what went wrong and recorded in the system log
under `notify:<channel>` (or `notify:ack-link` for a token too broken to say
which channel sent it), because a button that silently did nothing is
indistinguishable from one nobody pressed:

| Answer | Why |
|---|---|
| 403 | Forged, altered, or signed with a different secret |
| 410 | Genuine but expired |
| 409 | Already used, or the alarm was raised again since, or there's nothing left to acknowledge |
| 404 | The alarm no longer exists, or acknowledge links are off |

The token itself is never logged, never put in an audit event and never
returned by any API: for as long as it's valid it's a credential. It does sit in
the ntfy message, necessarily, so anyone who can read your ntfy topic can press
the button. Lock the topic down.

The endpoint answers with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` so the button also
works from the ntfy web app, which presses it from its own origin. That gives
nothing away: nothing on this route reads a cookie or a session.

## Escalation

Nobody acknowledged the alarm in N minutes, so the next person gets it. The
first page goes out exactly as it always did, to every channel whose floor the
alarm meets. Escalation is what happens after that, if the alarm is still
sitting there unacknowledged. A page that went to a phone nobody was holding is
the failure this exists for: at 03:00 the person on call is asleep, and the
alarm should not wait for them.

You set it up in **Settings, Alarm escalation**, or over the API
(`GET` and `PUT /api/notify/escalation`). It's admin only, because it holds
people's ntfy topics and decides who gets woken. Unlike the channels, which are
read from the environment when HotLoop starts, the policy is data you edit and
it takes effect when you save it. The channels it can use are the ones the
deployment already configured. Nothing new is added to the list of four, plus
the webhook and email.

### The policy

| Field | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|
| `enabled` | Off until you turn it on. An off policy escalates nothing |
| `minPriority` | The least severe alarm that escalates: `critical`, `high`, `medium` or `low`. Default `high`. A Medium alarm that's been sitting for an hour is a work order, not a 03:00 phone call |
| `contacts` | The people. Each has a `name`, and an `ntfyTopic`, `emails`, or both. Up to 50 |
| `steps` | Up to 10. Each has `afterMinutes` (1 to 1440) and who to tell: `contacts` by name, `channels` by name, or both |
| `repeatEveryMinutes`, `repeatTimes` | After the last step, send it again this often, this many more times (at most 20). Both zero for no repeat |

A **person** gets a notification of their own. Their `ntfyTopic` is a topic on
the ntfy server this HotLoop already publishes to, with the same login, so
their phone subscribes to a topic that is only theirs. Their `emails` go through
the SMTP relay HotLoop already has. A person with a topic needs ntfy configured,
and one with an address needs email configured, and the policy is refused with
that said if they aren't. On a server anybody can reach, a topic is a password:
make it long and random. The API shows topics to admins and nobody else, and
they are never in the logbook, the system log or an error.

A **channel** in a step is one of the deployment's own (`ntfy`, `gotify`,
`smtp`, `webhook`, `discord-webhook`, `discord`) and reaches whoever is on it:
the shared Discord channel, a Gotify app a crew shares, a webhook into
something that pages. The policy is refused if a step names one this HotLoop
hasn't configured, and the answer lists the ones it has.

### When things go out

A step is due `afterMinutes` after the one before it, and the first step
`afterMinutes` after the alarm was raised. It's a sum from the raise, not from
when the last send finished, so a slow relay or a restart doesn't stretch the
schedule you wrote. With steps of 5 and 10 and a repeat of 15 minutes, twice:

```
 0 min  alarm raised: the first page, as always
 5 min  step 1
15 min  step 2
30 min  step 2 again (repeat 1)
45 min  step 2 again (repeat 2), and that is the last
```

### What stops it

The chain is for one occurrence of one alarm, and it stops, with a row saying
why, when any of these happens:

- **Somebody acknowledges it.** From anywhere: the alarm screen, the
  Acknowledge button on ntfy or Discord, the API, an automation. They all end in
  the alarm engine, and before every step goes out the escalator asks the engine
  whether this occurrence is still unacknowledged. A hook that arrives late
  can't make it page an alarm somebody already answered.
- **It returns to normal.** The alarm is still on the alarm list needing
  somebody to acknowledge it, but nobody is woken up for something that fixed
  itself. That's a call I made on purpose; change the floor or the steps if you
  want a different one.
- **It's shelved.**
- **It trips again.** That's a new occurrence with its own chain, counted from
  its own raise. Yesterday's chain never pages for today's alarm.

An alarm somebody answers before step 1 is due leaves no trace in the
escalation trail at all, which is the system working.

### What arrives

An escalation is the alarm's own notification with its title changed and a line
added:

```
NOT ACKNOWLEDGED 15 min: Boiler Trip
Nobody has acknowledged this alarm in 15 minutes (step 2 of 4). boiler/Pressure hi 90 (now 95)
```

It keeps the alarm's priority, so a Critical one is still max priority on
Android. It carries the same signed Acknowledge button as the first page on
ntfy and Discord (see "Acknowledge links"), so the person it wakes can
acknowledge from where they were told. Gotify and email have no button. A
webhook gets HotLoop's usual JSON with `event` set to `escalated`.

A shared channel is paced like any other (see "Rate limits and summaries"), so a
power dip that leaves forty alarms unacknowledged escalates as one summary,
"40 alarms nobody has acknowledged", not forty pages and a ban. A person's own
notification is a send of its own.

### The audit trail

Every escalation is a row in the alarm's own trail, which is what the
[logbook](/iot/logbook/) reads, so it shows up there with no extra setup, filed
under the alarm with the actor `escalation`:

```
alarm Boiler Trip escalated: boiler/Pressure hi 90 (now 95) (note: step 1 of 2: nobody acknowledged it in 5 min; notified Ana (email), Ana (ntfy))
alarm Boiler Trip escalation-ended: boiler/Pressure hi 90 (now 95) (note: escalation stopped after 1 sent: acknowledged by notify:ntfy)
```

`GET /api/alarms/events` and the logbook's `alarm` kind carry the same rows as
types `escalated` and `escalation-ended`. A step that reached nobody says so in
capitals (`NOBODY WAS REACHED`) with each failure after it, and the chain
carries on to the next step anyway: one dead relay shouldn't stop the page that
goes out a different way. Saving the policy is in the system log without the
topics.

### Restarts, and where it runs

The chains live in memory, so a restart at 03:00 in the middle of one can't be
allowed to lose it. When HotLoop starts it looks at every alarm still
unacknowledged, reads how many steps the audit rows say went out for that
occurrence, and carries on from there: it doesn't send step 1 again and it
doesn't skip step 2. A step that came due while HotLoop was down goes out in
the first few seconds after it's back. A step that was in flight when the
process was killed may go out twice, which is the right way round to be wrong
for an alarm.

A saved policy applies to alarms raised after you save it. A restart picks up
every alarm still unacknowledged, whenever it was raised.

The Gateway runs it. An `--mcp-stdio` helper doesn't, so one alarm is never
escalated by two processes.

### Tested against the lab's real servers

`TestEscalationAgainstTheLabsRealServers` (`internal/api`) raises a real alarm
on a real Modbus register and pages a real ntfy, a real Gotify and a real
Mailpit, with the policy saved through the API. Ana's escalation lands on her
own ntfy topic and in her own mailbox, with an Acknowledge button; the button is
pressed from the message ntfy holds, with no session, and the alarm is
acknowledged and nothing more goes out, not to Bo and not to Gotify. The alarm
trips again and runs the whole chain: Ana at 5 minutes, then Bo's email and the
Gotify channel at 15. The escalation rows are read back out of the logbook. The
unit tests (`internal/notify/escalate_test.go`) cover the schedule, every way a
chain stops, a floor, an off policy, a step that reaches nobody and a restart
half way through, and the policy's validation.

The clock is the one thing that isn't real: the escalator reads a clock the test
moves forward by the minute, because a schedule in minutes is not something a
test should wait for. **Not verified**: a real run with real minutes on a real
plant, and what a given phone does with the notification once ntfy has it. The
escalation to a Discord channel carries the same buttons as a raise, checked
against the Discord stand-in like the rest of Discord, not the real service.

## TLS on the SMTP channel

The channel upgrades to TLS via STARTTLS automatically whenever the relay
advertises the extension, regardless of any setting below. This is not
optional behavior to opt into: Go's own `net/smtp.PlainAuth` refuses to
transmit a username and password over a connection that is not already TLS
(or to a server literally named `localhost`), and essentially every real
provider that requires authentication, Gmail, SendGrid, Mailgun, an ISP's
relay, requires STARTTLS on port 587 or implicit TLS on 465 (see below) to
get there. A relay with no
authentication configured, reachable on an isolated network, may not offer
STARTTLS at all, and this channel does not require it in that case.

`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_TLS` does not turn the upgrade on, it turns the
*absence* of it into a hard failure: if set and the relay does not advertise
STARTTLS, `Send` refuses before ever attempting `AUTH`, rather than quietly
authenticating in plaintext against a relay that merely happens to be
reachable as `localhost`. `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY` skips
certificate verification on the upgrade, the same escape hatch
`HOTLOOP_EDGE_PUBLISH_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY` and `HOTLOOP_FLEET_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY`
already provide for their own MQTT connections, for a relay presenting a
self-signed certificate.

### Implicit TLS, port 465

A relay on port 465 expects the whole connection to be TLS from the first byte
(RFC 8314), not a plaintext greeting and an upgrade. HotLoop used to only do
the upgrade, so on 465 the first thing it said was plaintext to a relay
waiting for a TLS handshake and the send died. Now **port 465 is implicit TLS**
and every other port is STARTTLS as before, with no setting to touch:

```
HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_PORT=465
```

If a relay does implicit TLS on a port of its own, or speaks STARTTLS on 465,
`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_IMPLICIT_TLS` says which, `true` or `false`, and wins over
the port. In the Helm chart set it under `extraEnv`. Everything else is the
same on both: the username and password go over the encrypted connection,
`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_TLS` is met by it (there is nothing to require), and
`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY` skips the certificate check on its
handshake. The relay's certificate is checked unless you turn that off.
Scheduled reports use the same relay settings and so the same rule.

If the handshake fails, the error says so and names
`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_IMPLICIT_TLS=false`, which is what a relay that starts in
plaintext needs.

Proved against a real SMTP server library with a TLS-only listener, and against
Mailpit run with `--smtp-require-tls`, the pinned lab version v1.31.2. Not
verified against a commercial provider's 465 endpoint.

## One SMTP code path, shared with scheduled reports

Since 4.14.0 the alarm channel sends through `notify.SendMessage`, a general
function that sends one message, with optional attachments, to a list of
recipients. Scheduled reports (see [REPORTS.md](/gateway/reports/)) send their CSV and
HTML files through the same function and the same relay settings
(`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_HOST`, `_PORT`, `_USERNAME`, `_PASSWORD`, `_FROM`, `_TLS`,
`_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY`), so there is one place that dials, upgrades with STARTTLS,
authenticates, and decides what a header may contain. Only the relay is shared:
`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_ENABLED`, `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_ENABLED`, and
`HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_TO` are about alarms, and a relay configured for reports
does not turn the alarm channel on.

Two behaviors of the alarm email changed, both in the direction of safety. The
sender and every recipient are now validated as plain addresses before anything
is dialed, where before a malformed one failed at the relay. And a subject with
non-ASCII characters is sent as an RFC 2047 encoded word instead of raw UTF-8.
For an ordinary ASCII alarm the message is the same bytes as before apart from
the `Date` header, which `TestAlarmMessageBytesAreUnchanged` pins. An alarm name
that contains a control character is flattened to spaces rather than refused,
because a page has to go out whatever an alarm is called.

## Priority floors

Each channel has its own `MinPriority`, the least severe alarm priority it
still fires for. `model.AlarmPriority` runs 1 (Critical, most severe) to 4
(Low), so "High and above" is `MinPriority = 2`: an alarm meets a channel's
floor when its own priority number is less than or equal to the floor.
A webhook configured for Critical-only and an SMTP relay configured for
Medium-and-above can watch the same alarm engine and fire on entirely
different sets of alarms, nothing requires them to agree.

## What it is not

**Not a live-reload of the channels.** Channels are read once, from
configuration, at process start, the same as `EdgePublishConfig` and
`FleetConfig`. Changing `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_*` needs a restart to take effect, there is no API to add or remove a channel at runtime in this MVP. The
escalation policy is the exception: who is told next, and when, is data you edit
and it takes effect when you save it (see "Escalation").

**Not a table of its own.** Every notification attempt, success or
failure, is written through `runtime.Manager.Event`, the same generic
audit-event mechanism every alarm and fleet action already logs through.
There was no need invented for a dedicated `notifications` table for a
feature this size; the system log already answers "was a notification sent,
and did it work."

**Not a durable queue.** Retries are bounded (three attempts, 30 seconds,
see "Retries") and held alarms live in memory until their summary goes out. A
page that still fails is logged and audited and the dispatcher moves on. An
alarm that stays raised because nobody acknowledged it is still visible on the
alarms screen and in `alarm_events` regardless of whether a page ever arrived:
the notification is a convenience on top of the alarm system, not a
replacement for it.

## Configuration

| Variable | Default | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_ENABLED` | `false` | The feature is off until this is set |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_WEBHOOK_ENABLED` | `false` | |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_WEBHOOK_URL` | n/a | Required when the webhook channel is enabled. Must be `http://` or `https://` |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_WEBHOOK_MIN_PRIORITY` | `high` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low`, or `1`-`4` |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_ENABLED` | `false` | |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_HOST` | n/a | Required when the SMTP channel is enabled |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_PORT` | `25` | |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_USERNAME` / `_PASSWORD` | n/a | Optional. Omit both for an anonymous relay |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_FROM` | n/a | Required when the SMTP channel is enabled |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_TO` | n/a | Required when the SMTP channel is enabled. Comma-separated addresses |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_TLS` | `false` | Require the relay to offer STARTTLS; see "TLS on the SMTP channel" above, STARTTLS is used automatically whenever offered regardless of this setting |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY` | `false` | Skip certificate verification on the STARTTLS upgrade, or on the handshake of implicit TLS. Per-deployment opt-in; never set this by default |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_IMPLICIT_TLS` | `true` on port 465, otherwise `false` | TLS from the first byte instead of STARTTLS; see "Implicit TLS, port 465". Set it to override the port |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_MIN_PRIORITY` | `high` | Same values as the webhook's |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_NTFY_ENABLED` | `false` | |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_NTFY_URL` | none | Required. The server alone, `https://ntfy.example.com`, no path |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_NTFY_TOPIC` | none | Required. 1 to 64 letters, digits, `-` and `_`. On a public server it's the password |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_NTFY_TOKEN` | none | An ntfy access token (`tk_...`), sent as a bearer token |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_NTFY_USERNAME` / `_PASSWORD` | none | Basic auth instead of a token. Not both |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_NTFY_ACK` | `true` | Put an Acknowledge button on every alarm (needs `HOTLOOP_PUBLIC_URL`) |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_NTFY_MIN_PRIORITY` | `high` | Same values as the webhook's |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_GOTIFY_ENABLED` | `false` | |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_GOTIFY_URL` | none | Required. `https://gotify.example.com` |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_GOTIFY_TOKEN` | none | Required. The application token Gotify gave you for HotLoop |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_GOTIFY_MIN_PRIORITY` | `high` | Same values as the webhook's |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_WEBHOOK_ENABLED` | `false` | |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL` | none | Required. The URL Discord's Copy Webhook URL gives. The whole of it is the password |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_WEBHOOK_CRITICAL_ROLE` | none | A role id to ping on Critical alarms |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_WEBHOOK_MIN_PRIORITY` | `high` | Same values as the webhook's |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_ENABLED` | `false` | |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN` | none | Required. The bot's token, alone, without `Bot ` in front |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_CHANNEL` | none | Required. The channel id to post in |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_ACK_ROLES` | none | Comma-separated role ids whose members may press Acknowledge. **Empty is nobody** |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_SHELVE_ROLES` | none | The same for Shelve. **Empty is nobody** |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_USERS` | none | `discordUserId=hotloopUser`, comma-separated: whose actions are recorded under their HotLoop name |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_SHELVE` | `1h` | How long Shelve shelves for. At most `24h` |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_CRITICAL_ROLE` | none | A role id to ping on Critical alarms |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_BOT_MIN_PRIORITY` | `high` | Same values as the webhook's |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_DISCORD_API_URL` | `https://discord.com/api/v10` | Only to send the bot's requests through a proxy |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_<CHANNEL>_BURST` / `_REFILL` | per channel | The rate limit; see "Rate limits and summaries". `<CHANNEL>` is `WEBHOOK`, `SMTP`, `NTFY`, `GOTIFY`, `DISCORD_WEBHOOK` or `DISCORD_BOT` |
| `HOTLOOP_PUBLIC_URL` | none | The address a phone reaches HotLoop at, base path included. Needed for tap-to-open and the Acknowledge button |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_ACK_SECRET` | generated | Signs acknowledge links. At least 32 characters. Unset: generated once and kept in the database |
| `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_ACK_TTL` | `12h` | How long an acknowledge link works. At most `168h` |

In the Helm chart these are under `notify.ntfy`, `notify.gotify`,
`notify.discordWebhook`, `notify.discordBot`, `notify.ackSecret`,
`notify.ackTtl` and the top-level `publicUrl`. Tokens, passwords and the
Discord webhook URL go into a Secret the chart manages, or name your own with
`existingSecret`.

## API

| Route | Permission | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/notify/test` | `notify.test` | Sends a synthetic test notification through every configured channel right now |
| `POST /api/notify/ack/{token}` | none; the token is the authorization | Acknowledges the alarm occurrence the token was issued for. See "Acknowledge links" |
| `GET /api/notify/escalation` | `notify.escalation` | The escalation policy, the channels a step may name, and the chains open right now. See "Escalation" |
| `PUT /api/notify/escalation` | `notify.escalation` | Replaces the whole policy. Refused with the reason if a step names nobody or a channel that isn't configured |
| `GET /api/diagnostics` | `status.read` | Under `notify.channels`, each channel's standing: whether Discord has refused it (and why, and since when), and the Discord bot's Gateway connection |

`notify.escalation` is admin-only the same way. Reading the policy needs it too,
because it holds people's ntfy topics.

`notify.test` is admin-only, granted by the wildcard the admin role already
carries and deliberately not added to the operator role's permission list, sending a real external message and spending whatever quota a paging
provider or SMTP relay allows is closer in kind to `fleet.restart` and
`fleet.config` (also admin-only, also "do something to the outside world
right now") than to a read, the same narrowing this app already applies to
those two.

The response reports each channel's own outcome rather than a single
pass/fail for the request:

```json
{
  "results": [
    {"channel": "webhook", "success": true},
    {"channel": "smtp", "success": false, "error": "dial smtp server mail.example.com:587: i/o timeout"}
  ]
}
```

## What has and has not been verified

**Tested**, not **verified**, see this repo's own distinction between the
two. The webhook channel is tested against a real `net/http/httptest` server:
the exact JSON body, an unreachable URL failing within its bounded context
rather than hanging, and a non-2xx response surfacing as an error rather than
a false success. The SMTP channel is tested against two real SMTP servers, [axllent/mailpit](https://github.com/axllent/mailpit), run via Podman, never
Docker, with the message's actual arrival, subject, body and recipients
confirmed afterward through Mailpit's own HTTP API, not just that `Send`
returned `nil`:

- A bare instance with no authentication, proving the ordinary path.
- A second instance configured to **require STARTTLS and a real login**
  (Mailpit's `--smtp-require-starttls` and `--smtp-auth-file`), proving the
  regression this feature actually shipped with once: `net/smtp.PlainAuth`
  silently refuses to send credentials over a connection that is not already
  TLS, so a channel configured with a username and password only ever worked
  against an unauthenticated local relay until the STARTTLS upgrade was
  added, the bare instance's tests could not have caught this, since
  `PlainAuth`'s refusal only triggers when a username is actually configured
  against a non-TLS, non-`localhost` connection. A third test proves
  `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_TLS` is a real refusal, pointed at a relay that
  offers no STARTTLS at all, `Send` fails before ever attempting `AUTH`.

The dispatcher's priority-floor filtering and its raised-only firing are both
covered directly, with a fake in-package channel standing in for "some
channel," the same way `internal/fleet`'s tests use a real
`edgepublish.Publisher` to stand in for "some edge relay" rather than a
hand-rolled mock.

The webhook's failures are also tested for the URL: a Discord-shaped URL with a
token in the path and in the query, against a real server that refuses the
connection, one that answers 500 and one that never answers, through
`POST /api/notify/test`, and neither token turns up in the response, the log or
the audit event.

ntfy and Gotify are tested against the real servers, `binwiederhier/ntfy`
and `gotify/server`, pinned in `test/services/up.sh` and run in CI, with what
arrived read back through each server's own API, the way a phone gets it. The
ntfy server requires a login for everything, so bearer and basic auth are both
exercised for real. Covered: the title, priority, tags, tap URL and
Acknowledge button of a raised alarm; a flood of ten alarms through a budget of
three producing exactly three sends and one summary naming the other seven;
held alarms going out on shutdown; a 429 with `Retry-After` waited out and
retried (ntfy itself never sends `Retry-After`, so a small proxy in front of
the real server answers the first request with one); a 5xx retried on the
backoff; a `Retry-After` past the budget not waited on; a wrong token sent once,
never retried; and no token, password, topic or acknowledge link in any error,
log line or result. Gotify: every priority's mapping, the Markdown and the tap
URL, a summary, and a wrong token reported with Gotify's own reason and never
printed.

The Acknowledge button is tested end to end in `internal/api`: a real alarm on
a real Modbus register raises, the notification lands on the real ntfy, and the
button's own request, read back from ntfy, is fired at HotLoop with no session.
The alarm is acknowledged in the real engine, audited as `notify:ntfy`. A
forged link, a used one (also after a shelve and unshelve), one from an earlier
occurrence of the same alarm and an expired one are each refused and each
leave the alarm unacknowledged. Nothing in the log, the audit trail or the API
carries the ntfy token, the topic, the signing key or any link.

**Not verified**: an iPhone receiving a push from a self-hosted ntfy through
ntfy.sh's relay, and the ntfy and Gotify phone apps themselves. The tests prove
what the servers hold and what the button sends; what a given phone does with
it is the app's business.

The Discord channels have their own account of this; see "Discord", "What's
verified, and what needs a live run".

**Not verified** against any specific commercial paging provider's webhook
format (PagerDuty, Opsgenie, ntfy.sh, Pushover, Slack, Discord; see the
Webhook section above for which of those can't work with it at all) or against a
phone carrier's email-to-SMS gateway, those are real-world integrations this
app cannot certify from the inside, only document, the same honesty
`docs/FLEET.md` applies to NCMD authorization and a certified Sparkplug host.
Also not verified: implicit TLS (a relay expecting TLS from the first byte,
typically port 465), only STARTTLS's in-band upgrade of a plaintext
connection is supported, which covers the common case (port 587 or 25) but
not every relay an operator might point this at.
